tool.name: MLflow
tool.tagline: Track experiments, version models and evaluate ML and GenAI apps
tool.description: MLflow is an open-source platform for the machine learning lifecycle. It records experiment runs (parameters, metrics, artifacts), packages models in a standard format, manages versions in a model registry, serves models, and adds tracing and evaluation for LLM and agent applications. Teams use it to make ML work reproducible, comparable and deployable.

glossary.def: In MLflow, a named group of related runs, such as all training attempts for one project, so they can be compared side by side.
In MLflow, recording something into a run, such as a setting, a score, a file or a model, with calls like log_param or log_metric, so it is saved for later.
In MLflow, a setting that defined a run, such as the learning rate, recorded once per run with log_param. (In plain Python, a parameter is a named input of a function.)
A number that measures how well a model does, such as accuracy or error. In MLflow it is recorded in a run, optionally once per step so it can be drawn as a curve.
In MLflow, any file saved with a run, such as a chart, a settings file, a table of predictions or the model itself.
Where MLflow keeps the files of runs and models: a local folder by default, or online file storage on a team setup.
MLflow's catalogue of models: each saved model can get a name and numbered versions, so programs can ask for a model by name.
A movable label, such as champion, attached to one version of a registered model. Moving the label switches which version programs load.
A shared MLflow program, running on a machine the whole team can reach, that stores everyone's runs and models in one place.
The address that tells MLflow where to save and read runs: a local database file, or the web address of a tracking server.
The database where an MLflow server keeps its records: experiments, runs, parameters, metrics and model versions (files go to the artifact store).
MLflow recording a library's settings, scores and model automatically when you train, after one call to mlflow.autolog().
MLflow's name for support for one model library, such as scikit-learn or PyTorch: each flavor knows how to save and load that library's models.
MLflow's generic model interface: any saved model can be loaded as a pyfunc and used with the same predict() call, whatever library built it.
In MLflow 3, a saved model with its own ID (m-...), its own parameters and metrics, and links to the runs that created or evaluated it.
An address MLflow uses to find a saved model, such as models:/m-123, models:/churn/3 or models:/churn@champion.
A few real rows of input saved with a model, so MLflow and other people can see what the model expects and test-load it.
A description saved with an MLflow model of what goes in and what comes out: the names and types of its input columns and outputs.
An MLflow run started inside another run. The outer one is the parent run and the inner ones are its child runs, shown grouped in the UI.
In MLflow, a record of one request through an AI app: every step it took, what went into and out of each step, and how long each took.
One step inside a trace, such as a single LLM call or a document search, with its inputs, outputs and timing.
In MLflow, a function that grades one answer of an AI app, for example by checking its length or comparing it with the expected answer.
An LLM given written instructions to grade another app's answers, for example for correctness or politeness.
The most popular Python library for classic machine learning. Every model in it is trained with fit() and used with predict().
The table type of the pandas library: named columns and numbered rows, like a spreadsheet inside a Python program.
A popular Python library for loading, cleaning and analysing tables of data.
Training a model many times with different hyperparameter values to find the combination that scores best.
A table that shows, for a model that picks categories, how often each true category was predicted as each category, so you see which ones get mixed up.
A saved copy of a model partway through training, so you can keep the best version or resume later.
Examples kept back from training and from all tuning, used only once at the very end to get a final, honest score. Unlike the validation set, nothing is adjusted to suit it.

concepts.name: Machine learning in plain words
concepts.summary: What training, a model, a validation set, a metric and a hyperparameter are: the ideas MLflow keeps track of.
concepts.why: MLflow records machine learning work, and every later lesson uses these few words.
concepts.body:
Imagine you want a program that guesses whether a customer will cancel their subscription. Writing the rules by hand ("if they haven't opened the app for 30 days...") gets hard fast. **Machine learning** takes another route: you show the computer many past examples, with the right answers, and let it find the pattern itself.

Those examples are the **training data**. Finding the pattern in them is called **training**.

What comes out of training is a **machine learning model**, usually just called a model: a bundle of learned numbers plus a formula that turns a new customer's details into a prediction. Using a finished model on new data is called **inference**.

How do you know a model is any good? You keep some examples out of training and check the model's predictions on them. While you are still trying out changes, you check on a **validation set**.

A **test set** is different: a second group of examples kept back the whole time and used only once, at the very end, for the final score. Because nothing was adjusted to suit it, that score shows how the model will do on truly new data.

A score like the share of correct answers (accuracy) is a **metric**.

Before training you also choose settings that shape how the model learns, such as how deep a decision tree (a model that asks a chain of yes/no questions) may grow, or how big each learning step is (the **learning rate**). Such settings are **hyperparameters**. Finding good ones means training many times with different values, and keeping track of all those attempts is exactly what MLflow is for.

In Python, the most common library for this kind of classic machine learning is **scikit-learn**. Every model in it works the same way: create the model object, call `fit(X, y)` to train it on inputs `X` and correct answers `y`, then call `predict(X_new)` to get predictions.

The inputs are usually a table: one row per example, one column per input, such as age or number of visits.

In Python such tables usually come as a **DataFrame**, the table type of the popular **pandas** library. You'll often see `X.head(3)`, which means "the first three rows of the table".
concepts.code:
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

# 150 flowers: 4 measurements each (X, a DataFrame) and the species as the answer (y)
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)

# keep a quarter of the flowers aside as the validation set
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)

model = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3)   # max_depth is a hyperparameter
model.fit(X_train, y_train)                   # training
preds = model.predict(X_val)                  # inference on unseen flowers

accuracy = (preds == y_val).mean()            # a metric: share of correct answers
print(round(accuracy, 2))                     # 0.97
takeaways: Training finds a pattern in example data and produces a model; using the model on new data is inference
Judge a model with a metric on a validation set it never trained on
Hyperparameters are settings you choose before training; tuning them means many training attempts
pitfalls: Measuring accuracy on the same examples the model trained on, which makes it look better than it really is.

quiz.q: While trying out changes to a model trained on 800 examples, you check it after each change on 200 other examples it never trained on. What are those 200 called?
quiz.explain: Examples held back from training and used to check the model while you keep adjusting it form the validation set; a separate test set is saved for one final score.

quiz.q: Which of these is a hyperparameter?
options: The model's accuracy on the validation set
The maximum depth you allow a decision tree to grow
One row of the training data
quiz.explain: A hyperparameter is a setting chosen before training; accuracy is a metric, and rows are data.

concepts.name: What MLflow does
concepts.summary: The big picture: MLflow records your training attempts, saves and versions models, and shows it all in a page you open locally.
concepts.why: Knowing the parts tells you which one solves your current problem, from comparing attempts to sharing a model.
concepts.body:
Training a good model is rarely one attempt. You try different hyperparameters, different data and different libraries, dozens of times over weeks. A month later someone asks "which settings gave us that 0.91 accuracy?" and the answer is lost in old scripts and file names. **MLflow** is a Python library, with a web page to browse the results, that keeps that record for you.

Its core idea is simple. Each training attempt is a **run**. During the run, your code records what went into it and what came out; MLflow calls this **logging**. Related runs are grouped in an **experiment**, such as "churn model".

A run can record three kinds of things: parameters (the settings it used), metrics (scores such as accuracy) and **artifacts** (any files, like a chart or the saved model).

Once a model is good, MLflow can save it in a standard package, so anyone can load it and call `predict` without your training code. The **Model Registry** then gives saved models names and version numbers, so other programs can ask for "the current churn model".

MLflow can also run a saved model as a small web service that other programs send data to, and it can record step by step what apps built on large language models (**LLMs**, the AI behind chatbots) are doing. Later lessons cover each part.

Install it with `pip install mlflow`. With no setup, MLflow saves everything into a file called `mlflow.db` in the folder you run your script from. That file is a small **database**: a store of records that programs can search and update quickly.

To look at your runs, start MLflow's web page from a terminal in that same folder:

```bash
mlflow ui --port 5000
```

Then open `http://localhost:5000`. **localhost** is the name your computer uses for itself, so the page comes from your own machine. This **user interface** (UI) lets you browse experiments, compare runs and see charts.

For a team, one shared **tracking server** replaces the local file so everyone sees the same runs (a later lesson). Your code stays the same; only the **tracking URI**, the address that tells MLflow where to save, changes.
concepts.code:
import mlflow

print(mlflow.__version__)          # 3.x
print(mlflow.get_tracking_uri())   # sqlite:///.../mlflow.db  (the local default)

mlflow.set_experiment("hello-mlflow")      # group runs under this name
with mlflow.start_run():                   # one run = one attempt
    mlflow.log_param("model", "baseline")  # a setting it used
    mlflow.log_metric("accuracy", 0.81)    # a score it got

# Then, in a terminal in the same folder:
#   mlflow ui --port 5000      -> open http://localhost:5000
takeaways: A run records one training attempt: its parameters, metrics and artifacts; an experiment groups runs
Saved models get a standard format, and the Model Registry gives them names and versions
By default everything goes into `mlflow.db` in the current folder; `mlflow ui` shows it
pitfalls: Starting `mlflow ui` in a different folder from your scripts and seeing no runs, because the local `mlflow.db` lives in the folder the script ran in.

quiz.q: Which part of MLflow lets other programs ask for 'the current churn model' by a stable name instead of a file path?
quiz.explain: The registry gives saved models names and versions (plus movable labels), so programs refer to a name rather than to a particular file.

concepts.name: Runs, params, metrics and tags
concepts.summary: Record each training attempt's settings, scores over time and labels inside a run, grouped by experiment.
concepts.why: Recording the same things every time is what lets you compare attempts weeks later.
concepts.body:
An experiment groups related runs, for example one per project. `mlflow.set_experiment("churn")` picks one by name, creating it if it doesn't exist yet.

A run is opened with a context manager, just like a file. The `with` block makes sure the run is closed properly, even if your code raises an exception inside it:

```python
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="rf-depth-8"):
    ...
```

Inside the run you log three kinds of information:

- **Parameters** are the settings that define the run, logged once with `log_param` or `log_params(dict)`. They are stored as strings, and logging the same name again with a different value is an error.
- **Metrics** are numbers that may change as the run goes on, logged with `log_metric` or `log_metrics(dict)`. An optional `step` number turns repeated values into a curve in the UI.
- **Tags** are free-form labels such as the data version, the git commit or the owner (`set_tag`, `set_tags`). MLflow adds a few itself, like the script name and the user.

Why steps? Many models train in rounds, and one full pass over the training data is an **epoch**. After each one you can measure the model's **loss function**: a score of how wrong it still is, where lower is better. Logging `val_loss` (the loss on the validation set) with `step=epoch` shows whether training is still improving.

The `with ... as run` form gives you the run object, and `run.info.run_id` is its unique ID, used to fetch results later with `mlflow.get_run`. When the block ends, the run's status is `FINISHED`, or `FAILED` if an exception escaped. Without a `with` block, call `mlflow.end_run()` yourself.

Log a parameter for everything that affects the result, including the data version and the **random seed** (the starting number for the program's random choices; the same seed gives the same choices). A run without them can be looked at but not reproduced.
concepts.code:
import mlflow

mlflow.set_experiment("churn-model")

with mlflow.start_run(run_name="gbm-lr-0.1") as run:
    mlflow.log_params({"learning_rate": 0.1, "max_depth": 4, "seed": 42})
    mlflow.set_tags({"data_version": "2026-10-01", "owner": "ml-team"})
    for epoch in range(3):                       # one value per epoch -> a curve
        mlflow.log_metric("val_loss", 0.9 / (epoch + 1), step=epoch)
    mlflow.log_metric("val_auc", 0.87)          # a single final score

finished = mlflow.get_run(run.info.run_id)
print(finished.info.status)          # FINISHED
print(finished.data.params)          # {'learning_rate': '0.1', 'max_depth': '4', 'seed': '42'}
print(finished.data.metrics["val_loss"])   # 0.3  (the latest value)
takeaways: Use `with mlflow.start_run()` so runs always close with the right status
Parameters are logged once, as strings; metrics can be logged many times with a step
Tag runs with data version, commit and owner so you can filter them later
pitfalls: Logging a value that changes, like the loss after each epoch, with log_param: the second call fails. Use log_metric.

quiz.q: You call mlflow.log_param('lr', 0.1) and later in the same run mlflow.log_param('lr', 0.01). What happens?
options: MLflow raises an error because a parameter can be set only once per run
Both values are stored as a history
The second call is silently ignored
quiz.explain: Parameters are write-once per run; values that change belong in metrics.

concepts.name: Logging artifacts
concepts.summary: Store files, charts, dicts, text and tables alongside a run, and read them back later.
concepts.why: Charts, lists of the inputs used and sample predictions explain a run far better than a few numbers.
concepts.body:
Numbers don't tell the whole story. A chart of the model's mistakes, the list of input columns it used, or a sample of its predictions often explains a run better. Any file you attach to a run is an artifact, and MLflow keeps it in the run's **artifact store**: a local folder by default, or online file storage once your team sets up a tracking server.

Ways to log them:

- `mlflow.log_artifact("report.html")` uploads one file; `log_artifacts("plots/")` uploads a whole folder. `artifact_path="eval"` puts them in a subfolder.
- `mlflow.log_dict(d, "config.json")` and `mlflow.log_text(s, "notes.md")` save a dict or a string as a file directly, with no temporary file on your disk.
- `mlflow.log_figure(fig, "roc.png")` saves a chart made with matplotlib or plotly, the popular Python charting libraries.
- `mlflow.log_image(image, key="samples", step=epoch)` saves pictures, optionally one per step.
- `mlflow.log_table(data=..., artifact_file="preds.json")` saves a table (a dict of columns or a DataFrame) that you can view and compare in the UI.

To read them back, `mlflow.artifacts.download_artifacts(run_id=..., artifact_path="config.json")` copies a file to your computer and returns its path. `mlflow.artifacts.load_dict` and `load_text` read straight from an address like `runs:/<run id>/config.json`. To list a run's files, use `MlflowClient`, MLflow's lower-level Python class with a method for almost everything: `MlflowClient().list_artifacts(run_id)`.

Keep artifacts purposeful. A big **dataset** (a collection of data, like a table of a million customers) belongs in its own storage; log only where it lives, or a version label, as a tag. Models are saved with `log_model` (the next lessons) rather than `log_artifact`, so MLflow also records how to load them.
concepts.code:
import json
import mlflow

with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    mlflow.log_dict({"features": ["age", "tenure"], "target": "churn"}, "config.json")
    mlflow.log_text("Baseline with two input columns.", "notes/summary.txt")
    mlflow.log_table(data={"id": [1, 2], "pred": [0.2, 0.9]}, artifact_file="preds.json")
    with open("threshold.json", "w") as f:      # an ordinary file on disk...
        json.dump({"threshold": 0.5}, f)
    mlflow.log_artifact("threshold.json", artifact_path="eval")   # ...copied into the run

from mlflow import MlflowClient
print(sorted(a.path for a in MlflowClient().list_artifacts(run.info.run_id)))
# ['config.json', 'eval', 'notes', 'preds.json']

cfg = mlflow.artifacts.load_dict(f"runs:/{run.info.run_id}/config.json")
print(cfg["target"])    # churn
takeaways: Artifacts are files stored with a run, in a local folder or online storage
`log_dict`, `log_text`, `log_figure` and `log_table` save objects without temporary files
Read them back with the `mlflow.artifacts` helpers and `runs:/<id>/path` addresses
pitfalls: Logging huge raw datasets as artifacts on every run, which fills up storage; log where the data lives instead.

quiz.q: Which call stores a matplotlib chart with a run without you saving it to a file first?
quiz.explain: log_figure turns the chart into an image file inside the run's artifacts; log_artifact needs a path to an existing file.

concepts.name: Autologging
concepts.summary: Record parameters, metrics and models automatically for scikit-learn, XGBoost, PyTorch Lightning and more.
concepts.why: One line gives you complete runs, so nothing important is forgotten.
concepts.body:
Writing `log_param` and `log_metric` for every setting gets tedious, and it's easy to forget one. `mlflow.autolog()` turns on **autologging**: MLflow hooks into supported libraries so that their training calls record themselves.

For scikit-learn, every call to `fit` creates a run (or uses the one that is open) and logs:

- every hyperparameter of the model object, read from its `get_params()`,
- metrics measured on the training data: for a **classification** model (one that picks a category, like spam or not spam) accuracy and similar scores; for a model that predicts a number, its average error,
- the trained model itself, ready to load later,
- for automatic searches such as `GridSearchCV`, which tries every combination of the values you list, the best values plus a separate run for each candidate.

Each library also has its own version with extra options, e.g. `mlflow.sklearn.autolog(log_models=False)`. Supported libraries include scikit-learn, XGBoost, LightGBM, Keras, PyTorch Lightning and Spark. For libraries that call LLMs, such as OpenAI's, autologging records traces (step-by-step records of each call) instead of training metrics; a later lesson covers them.

Autologging mixes with manual logging: inside your own `with mlflow.start_run():` block, your extra `log_metric` calls land in the same run. Scores on the validation set are not logged by `fit`, because `fit` never sees that data. MLflow logs them when you score the model afterwards, for example with `model.score(X_val, y_val)`.

Call `mlflow.autolog()` before you train, and switch it off with `mlflow.autolog(disable=True)`. It's ideal while exploring. For the code that builds the models your product really uses, many teams log explicitly so that every run's contents are deliberate.
concepts.code:
import mlflow
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

mlflow.sklearn.autolog()                       # switch on before training
X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True)
X_tr, X_val, y_tr, y_val = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=0)

with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    model = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=50, max_depth=3, random_state=0)
    model.fit(X_tr, y_tr)                 # params, training metrics and model logged
    model.score(X_val, y_val)             # validation score logged too

r = mlflow.get_run(run.info.run_id)
print(r.data.params["max_depth"])         # 3
print(sorted(k for k in r.data.metrics if k.startswith("training_"))[:3])
# ['training_accuracy_score', 'training_f1_score', 'training_log_loss']
takeaways: `mlflow.autolog()` logs parameters, metrics and the model for supported libraries
Your own log calls inside the same run add to what was logged automatically
For LLM libraries, autologging records traces instead of training metrics
pitfalls: Turning autologging on after the model was already trained, so nothing gets recorded.

quiz.q: Where do autologged scikit-learn metrics come from by default?
options: From the training data, plus any scoring calls you make after fit
From extra training runs MLflow starts on its own
They are not logged; only parameters are
quiz.explain: Autologging measures the model on its training data when fit runs, and records later scores when you call scoring functions such as model.score.

concepts.name: Logging and loading models
concepts.summary: Save a trained model with log_model, load it back as the original object or through MLflow's generic interface, and read model addresses.
concepts.why: A logged model carries the library versions it needs and how to call it, so others can use it without your training code.
concepts.body:
Saving a model with MLflow takes one call. MLflow has a module for each supported model library, and calls each one a **flavor**. Every flavor has a `log_model` function, e.g. `mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="model")` for scikit-learn.

In MLflow 3 this creates a **LoggedModel**: a saved model with its own ID, linked to the open run. The function returns a `ModelInfo` object whose `model_uri` is the model's address, like `models:/m-1a2b...`. Such a **model URI** is how you point at a model when you load it.

Behind the scenes MLflow writes a folder containing:

- `MLmodel`, a small text file listing the flavors, the expected inputs and other details,
- the model itself, saved as a file of bytes,
- `requirements.txt` and similar files listing the exact library versions it needs,
- an optional input example.

You can load it back two ways:

- **The flavor's own loader**: `mlflow.sklearn.load_model(uri)` gives back the original scikit-learn object, with all its methods.
- **pyfunc**: `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(uri)` gives a generic wrapper whose `predict(data)` works the same whatever library built the model. MLflow's own serving tools use it, and so can your code.

Model URIs you will see: `models:/<model_id>`; `runs:/<run_id>/<path>`, the older style; and `models:/<name>/<version>` or `models:/<name>@<alias>` for models in the Model Registry (a later lesson).

Always pass an **input example**: a few real rows of input. MLflow uses it to record what inputs the model expects, and it test-loads the saved model to check that it really predicts. The most common loading problem is different library versions on the machine that loads the model; the logged `requirements.txt` tells you what to install.
concepts.code:
import mlflow
from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge

X, y = load_diabetes(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
model = Ridge(alpha=0.5).fit(X, y)                # a simple model that predicts a number

with mlflow.start_run():
    info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="ridge", input_example=X.head(3))

print(info.model_uri.startswith("models:/"))   # True (MLflow 3 LoggedModel address)

native = mlflow.sklearn.load_model(info.model_uri)
print(type(native).__name__, native.alpha)     # Ridge 0.5

generic = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(info.model_uri)
print(generic.predict(X.head(2)).round(1))     # same predictions as native.predict
print(generic.metadata.get_input_schema().input_names()[:3])  # ['age', 'sex', 'bmi']: expected input columns
takeaways: `<flavor>.log_model(model, name=...)` saves a LoggedModel with its MLmodel file and library versions
Load with the flavor's loader for the original object, or with `mlflow.pyfunc` for a uniform `predict`
Pass an input example so MLflow records the expected inputs and test-loads the model
pitfalls: Loading a model on a machine with different library versions from the ones in its requirements.txt, which can fail or quietly change predictions.

options: A generic model wrapper with the same predict() for every library
quiz.explain: pyfunc is MLflow's library-independent interface, used by its serving tools and for scoring data in bulk.

concepts.name: Searching and comparing runs
concepts.summary: Find runs from code with filter strings and sorting, and compare them side by side in the UI.
concepts.why: Picking the best run, building reports and cleaning up old runs all start with search.
concepts.body:
`mlflow.search_runs()` returns a pandas DataFrame with one row per run and columns like `run_id`, `status`, `params.max_depth`, `metrics.val_auc` and `tags.owner`. (`val_auc` here is a common 0-to-1 quality score for models that pick between two answers; higher is better.)

```python
mlflow.search_runs(experiment_names=["churn"],
                   filter_string="metrics.val_auc > 0.85 and params.model = 'gbm'",
                   order_by=["metrics.val_auc DESC"], max_results=5)
```

The filter language is modelled on **SQL**, the standard language for asking a database questions:

- Prefixes: `metrics.`, `params.`, `tags.`, `attributes.` (e.g. `attributes.status = 'FINISHED'`, `attributes.start_time > ...` in milliseconds).
- Parameters and tags are strings, so compare them with quoted strings; metrics are numbers.
- Operators: `=`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `LIKE` and `ILIKE` (text patterns), `IN`, `IS NULL`, combined with `AND` (there is no `OR`).
- Names with spaces or dots need backticks: ``metrics.`val auc` ``.

`MlflowClient().search_runs(...)` returns `Run` objects instead of a DataFrame and hands results back one page at a time (**pagination**), which suits scripts that work through many runs.

In the UI, select runs and click **Compare** to see charts of each parameter against each metric, and their metric curves drawn on top of each other. Charts and tables can be grouped by tag or parameter, handy for a **hyperparameter search** (also called a sweep), where many runs differ in only a few settings.

Metric filters use the **latest** logged value of each metric; log a separate `best_val_auc` metric if you need to search on the best epoch.
concepts.code:
import mlflow

mlflow.set_experiment("search-demo")
for depth in [2, 4, 8]:
    with mlflow.start_run(run_name=f"depth-{depth}"):
        mlflow.log_params({"model": "tree", "max_depth": depth})
        mlflow.log_metric("val_auc", 0.70 + depth * 0.02)

best = mlflow.search_runs(
    experiment_names=["search-demo"],
    filter_string="params.model = 'tree' and metrics.val_auc > 0.75",
    order_by=["metrics.val_auc DESC"],
)
print(best[["params.max_depth", "metrics.val_auc"]].head(2).to_string(index=False))
# params.max_depth  metrics.val_auc
#                8             0.86
#                4             0.78
takeaways: `search_runs` returns a DataFrame with params., metrics. and tags. columns
Filter strings quote string values; metrics compare as numbers
Metric filters see the latest value, not the best
pitfalls: Comparing parameters as numbers, like params.max_depth > 4; parameters are strings, so compare them as strings or convert the column in pandas.

quiz.q: Which filter string is valid for runs whose parameter optimizer is adam?
quiz.explain: Use the params. prefix, a single = and a quoted string value.

concepts.name: Signatures and input examples
concepts.summary: Describe the inputs and outputs a model expects with a signature, so MLflow can reject bad input before predicting.
concepts.why: Checking inputs catches wrong or missing columns before they silently produce bad predictions.
concepts.body:
A **model signature** describes what a model takes in and gives back: the names and types of its input columns, of its outputs, and of optional extra settings called params. It's saved in the `MLmodel` file, shown in the UI, and checked every time the model is called through `pyfunc` or served as a web service.

Create one from data:

```python
from mlflow.models import infer_signature
signature = infer_signature(X_train, model.predict(X_train))
```

or let `log_model(..., input_example=X.head())` work it out for you. Most signatures are **column-based**: named, typed columns from a DataFrame or dict. Models that take grids of numbers, such as images, use **tensor-based** signatures instead. A **tensor** is a grid of numbers with any number of dimensions; the signature records its number type and shape, with `-1` for a size that can vary.

MLflow calls this checking **schema enforcement** (a **schema** is a description of how data is structured). On `predict` it does the following:

- Missing required columns raise an error; extra columns are dropped with a warning.
- Types are converted where it's safe (whole numbers to decimals) and rejected otherwise.
- Columns marked optional may be absent.

Params let callers change behaviour per call without changing the input data, e.g. `{"threshold": 0.7}`, or `max_tokens` (a limit on answer length) for an LLM. Declare them with `infer_signature(X, y, params={"threshold": 0.5})`; the default value comes from the signature.

Whole-number columns with missing values are a classic trap. pandas stores a missing value as a decimal "not a number", so such a column turns into decimals when the model is used, and a column logged as whole numbers fails the check. Convert such columns to float before training and logging.
concepts.code:
import mlflow
import pandas as pd
from mlflow.models import infer_signature
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X = pd.DataFrame({"age": [25.0, 40.0, 33.0, 51.0], "visits": [1.0, 5.0, 2.0, 8.0]})
y = [0, 1, 0, 1]
model = LogisticRegression().fit(X, y)

signature = infer_signature(X, model.predict(X))
print(signature.inputs)   # ['age': double (required), 'visits': double (required)]

with mlflow.start_run():
    info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="clf", signature=signature,
                                    input_example=X.head(2))

loaded = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(info.model_uri)
try:
    loaded.predict(pd.DataFrame({"age": [30.0]}))   # 'visits' missing
except mlflow.exceptions.MlflowException as e:
    print("rejected:", "visits" in str(e))           # rejected: True
takeaways: Signatures describe inputs, outputs and per-call params
pyfunc and served models check every call against the signature
Create it from real data with `infer_signature` or an input example
pitfalls: Training on whole-number columns that may have missing values later, so the check rejects the decimal columns pandas produces.

quiz.q: A served model's signature requires columns a and b. A request sends a, b and c. What happens by default?
options: c is passed to the model as an extra input
Column c is dropped and prediction goes ahead
quiz.explain: Extra columns are ignored with a warning; missing required ones would fail.

concepts.name: Model registry and aliases
concepts.summary: Register model versions under a name, point labels like champion at them, and load models by label.
concepts.why: The Model Registry separates using a model from training it: services load 'the champion' while you swap versions behind it.
concepts.body:
The Model Registry gives logged models a **registered model name** and automatically numbered **versions**. Register a model while logging it (`log_model(..., registered_model_name="churn")`) or afterwards:

```python
mv = mlflow.register_model(info.model_uri, "churn")
```

Each version links back to the run and logged model that produced it, so you can always see where it came from.

To mark which version is used where, attach a **model alias**: a movable label such as `champion`, `challenger` or `staging`. Each alias points at one version:

```python
client.set_registered_model_alias("churn", "champion", mv.version)
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/churn@champion")
```

Promoting a new model is just moving the alias. Going back to the old one (a **rollback**) is moving it back. Code that loads `@champion` never changes.

Older MLflow versions used fixed stages (`Staging`, `Production`) instead. They are **deprecated**: still there, but being phased out in favour of aliases and tags.

Other useful operations on `MlflowClient`:

- `set_model_version_tag` for notes like `validation_status=passed`.
- `get_model_version_by_alias`, `search_model_versions("name='churn'")`.
- Descriptions on models and versions, as documentation.

Many companies keep a development setup separate from **production** (the live system real users rely on). A common pattern is one registry per setup, or names prefixed by setup, and copying approved versions across with `client.copy_model_version`.
concepts.code:
import mlflow
from mlflow import MlflowClient
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
client = MlflowClient()

versions = []
for C in [0.1, 1.0]:
    with mlflow.start_run():
        m = LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)
        info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(m, name="clf", input_example=X.head(2))
    versions.append(mlflow.register_model(info.model_uri, "iris-clf").version)

client.set_registered_model_alias("iris-clf", "champion", versions[-1])
client.set_model_version_tag("iris-clf", versions[-1], "validated", "true")

champ = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/iris-clf@champion")
print(champ.predict(X.head(3)))                       # [0 0 0]
mv = client.get_model_version_by_alias("iris-clf", "champion")
print(mv.version == versions[-1], mv.tags)            # True {'validated': 'true'}
takeaways: Registered models have versions linked to the runs that produced them
Aliases (e.g. @champion) are movable labels; load with `models:/name@alias`
Promote or roll back by moving an alias; the old stages are deprecated
pitfalls: Writing a fixed version number into the code that uses the model, so every model update needs a code change and a new release.

quiz.q: How do you roll back production from version 7 to version 6 if services load models:/fraud@champion?
options: Change the services to load version 6
Point the champion alias at version 6
quiz.explain: Moving the alias changes what models:/fraud@champion resolves to without touching consumers.

concepts.name: Nested runs for tuning
concepts.summary: Organize a hyperparameter search as a parent run with one child run per attempt.
concepts.why: Searches produce dozens of runs; nesting keeps the experiment readable and the best attempt easy to find.
concepts.body:
A hyperparameter search is naturally a tree: one **parent run** for the search, and one **child run** for each combination tried. Create children with `nested=True` while the parent is open:

```python
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="search"):
    for params in grid:
        with mlflow.start_run(nested=True):
            ...
```

Children get the tag `mlflow.parentRunId`, and the UI shows them folded under the parent. Log the search setup and the best result on the parent, so the parent alone answers "what did this search find?".

Patterns that work well:

- Log each child's params and its score on the validation set; log the best params and score to the parent at the end.
- Find the children with `filter_string=f"tags.mlflow.parentRunId = '{parent_id}'"`.
- With Optuna, a tuning library, start a nested run inside the objective function (the function Optuna calls once per attempt).

If attempts run at the same time in several **threads** (parts of one program that run side by side), pass `parent_run_id=` to `start_run` explicitly. MLflow remembers the open run separately for each thread, so a new thread doesn't know about the parent.

scikit-learn autologging does all this for you with `GridSearchCV` and `RandomizedSearchCV` (which tries random combinations), creating child runs for the top candidates (limited by `max_tuning_runs`).

Keep the number of metrics per child small; thousands of child runs, each with many per-step metrics, make the UI slow.
concepts.code:
import mlflow

def train(lr, depth):                    # stand-in for real training
    return 0.9 - abs(lr - 0.1) - abs(depth - 4) * 0.01

mlflow.set_experiment("tuning-demo")
with mlflow.start_run(run_name="grid-search") as parent:
    best = None
    for lr in [0.01, 0.1, 0.3]:
        for depth in [2, 4]:
            with mlflow.start_run(nested=True):
                score = train(lr, depth)
                mlflow.log_params({"lr": lr, "depth": depth})
                mlflow.log_metric("val_score", score)
            if best is None or score > best[0]:
                best = (score, lr, depth)
    mlflow.log_metric("best_val_score", best[0])
    mlflow.log_params({"best_lr": best[1], "best_depth": best[2]})

kids = mlflow.search_runs(filter_string=f"tags.mlflow.parentRunId = '{parent.info.run_id}'")
print(len(kids), best)                   # 6 (0.9, 0.1, 4)
takeaways: Use a parent run per search and `nested=True` child runs per attempt
Record the best params and score on the parent
Children carry the `mlflow.parentRunId` tag, so you can search for them
pitfalls: Starting child runs from other threads without passing parent_run_id, which produces stray top-level runs.

quiz.q: How can you list all trials of a sweep whose parent run ID is p?
options: Search for run names starting with p
quiz.explain: Child runs are tagged with mlflow.parentRunId, which search filters can use.

concepts.name: Remote tracking server
concepts.summary: Share experiments across a team with mlflow server, a database for run records and online storage for files.
concepts.why: A local mlflow.db works for one person; a team needs one shared server so everyone sees the same runs and models.
concepts.body:
`mlflow server` starts a long-running program, a **server**, that other machines reach over the network. It offers what your local setup offers: the tracking functions your code calls, the Model Registry and the UI. It keeps two kinds of data in two places.

The **backend store** holds the records: experiments, runs, params, metrics and registered models. For a team it's a real database such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, e.g. `--backend-store-uri postgresql://user:pw@db/mlflow`. SQLite, the single-file database behind `mlflow.db`, is fine on one machine.

The artifact store holds the files and models. For a team it's usually **object storage**: an online file-storage service such as Amazon S3, Google Cloud Storage or Azure Blob, e.g. `--artifacts-destination s3://ml-artifacts`. A shared network drive also works.

By default the server passes files through for its users: your scripts upload and download artifacts via the server, which acts as a **proxy** (a go-between). The **clients**, here your scripts, then need no storage passwords of their own. Alternatively, clients can write to the storage directly if they have access.

Clients find the server through the tracking URI, set either:

- in code, with `mlflow.set_tracking_uri("http://mlflow.internal:5000")`, or
- with the **environment variable** `MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI` (a named setting the operating system hands to every program it starts), which keeps the address out of your code.

Protect a shared server. Serve it over **HTTPS**, the encrypted version of the web's protocol, so passwords and data can't be read on the way, and require users to sign in: MLflow has a built-in username-and-password mode (`--app-name basic-auth`), or a company sign-in gateway can sit in front of it.

For heavier use, run several copies of the server program with `--workers`. Back up the database regularly (the files live in object storage). New MLflow versions sometimes change the layout of the database's tables; apply those changes with `mlflow db upgrade <uri>`, after a backup.
concepts.code:
# Start a team server (shell):
#   mlflow server --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5000 \
#       --backend-store-uri postgresql://mlflow:secret@db:5432/mlflow \
#       --artifacts-destination s3://acme-ml-artifacts
#
# Clients: export MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI=http://mlflow.internal:5000
import os
import mlflow

uri = os.environ.get("MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI", "sqlite:///mlflow.db")
mlflow.set_tracking_uri(uri)
print(mlflow.get_tracking_uri())       # whichever store is configured

mlflow.set_experiment("shared-experiment")
with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    mlflow.log_metric("rmse", 3.2)
print(run.info.artifact_uri[:30])      # mlflow-artifacts:/... when files go through a server
takeaways: Backend store = database for run records; artifact store = object storage for files
With the default pass-through, users' machines need no storage passwords
Point code at the server with MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI rather than a hard-coded address
pitfalls: Running a shared server from a laptop with a local SQLite file, then losing the team's history when the laptop goes away.

quiz.q: In the default setup, where the server passes artifacts through, who needs write access to the S3 storage?
quiz.explain: With pass-through artifacts, scripts send files via the server, which is the only part that talks to S3.

concepts.name: Custom pyfunc models
concepts.summary: Wrap extra processing, several models or any Python logic as one MLflow model with PythonModel and artifacts.
concepts.why: Real predictors include input clean-up, thresholds and several models; a custom pyfunc ships them as one unit.
concepts.body:
When a model is more than one library object's `predict`, subclass `mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel`:

- `load_context(self, context)` runs once, when the model is loaded. `context.artifacts` maps names to the local paths of files you attached, such as a word list or a second model.
- `predict(self, context, model_input, params=None)` makes the predictions. `params` receives the per-call params declared in the signature.

Log it with `mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(name=..., python_model=MyModel(), artifacts={...}, pip_requirements=[...])`. The artifacts are copied into the model's folder, so the result is self-contained.

There are two ways to provide the model:

- An **instance** (`python_model=MyModel()`), which MLflow saves with cloudpickle, a more capable version of Python's **pickle** module for turning objects into bytes. Easy, but loading can break under different Python or library versions.
- **Models from code**: pass the path of a Python file that defines the model and calls `mlflow.models.set_model(MyModel())`. Nothing is pickled; the code itself is stored, which is more robust and readable. This is the recommended approach, especially for LLM apps and agents.

Type hints on `predict` (e.g. `model_input: list[str]`) let MLflow work out the signature and check inputs automatically.

Keep `predict` free of training logic and of **network requests** (calls to other services over the network) you cannot control, and pin every library it needs in `pip_requirements`: the serving environment is built from them.
concepts.code:
import mlflow
import pandas as pd

class ThresholdModel(mlflow.pyfunc.PythonModel):
    def load_context(self, context):
        cfg = mlflow.artifacts.load_dict(context.artifacts["config"])
        self.threshold = cfg["threshold"]

    def predict(self, context, model_input: pd.DataFrame, params=None):
        thr = (params or {}).get("threshold", self.threshold)
        score = model_input["a"] * 0.6 + model_input["b"] * 0.4
        return (score > thr).astype(int)

with mlflow.start_run() as run:
    mlflow.log_dict({"threshold": 0.5}, "config.json")
    info = mlflow.pyfunc.log_model(
        name="thresh", python_model=ThresholdModel(),
        artifacts={"config": f"runs:/{run.info.run_id}/config.json"},
        input_example=pd.DataFrame({"a": [0.9, 0.1], "b": [0.8, 0.2]}),
    )

m = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model(info.model_uri)
print(list(m.predict(pd.DataFrame({"a": [0.9, 0.1], "b": [0.8, 0.2]}))))   # [1, 0]
takeaways: Subclass PythonModel; load resources in `load_context`, infer in `predict`
Attach files via `artifacts` so the model is self-contained
Prefer models-from-code over pickled instances for robustness
pitfalls: Loading large resources inside predict on every call instead of once in load_context.

quiz.q: Where should a custom pyfunc load a 500 MB data file it needs for every prediction?
options: In load_context, from a path in context.artifacts
Download it from the internet in predict
At the top of predict, on every call
quiz.explain: load_context runs once when the model is loaded, and artifacts are bundled with the model.

concepts.name: Serving and deploying models
concepts.summary: Run a logged or registered model as a web service, package it as a Docker image, and score data in bulk.
concepts.why: The point of packaging a model is to run it somewhere else with the same behaviour.
concepts.body:
Any pyfunc model can run as a small web service: other programs send it data over **HTTP**, the protocol web browsers use, and get predictions back. You don't write any server code:

```bash
mlflow models serve -m "models:/churn@champion" -p 5001
```

This starts a server, using an environment built from the model's requirements (or the current one with `--env-manager local`). It answers on a few **endpoints**, the URL paths a service responds to:

- `POST /invocations` for predictions, accepting JSON such as `{"dataframe_split": {"columns": [...], "data": [[...]]}}`, `{"dataframe_records": [...]}`, or `{"inputs": ...}` for tensors, plus optional `"params"`;
- `GET /ping` and `/health` to check the service is up (**health checks**); `/version`.

To run it on other machines, `mlflow models build-docker -m <uri> -n churn-model` builds a **container image**: a packaged snapshot of the model, its libraries and the server. Tools like Docker or Kubernetes start it as a **container**, an isolated running copy, which answers on network port 8080. `mlflow models generate-dockerfile` writes the build recipe instead, so you can customise it.

Other ways to use a model:

- **Batch scoring**: predict for a whole file or table in one go. Load the model with `mlflow.pyfunc.load_model` in a scheduled job, or use `mlflow.pyfunc.spark_udf` to score Spark DataFrames spread over many machines.
- **Cloud platforms**: **plugins** for SageMaker, Azure ML, Databricks and others, via `mlflow deployments`.

Before you **deploy** a model (put it where real users or systems reach it), test it in isolation with `mlflow models predict -m <uri> -i input.json` or `mlflow.models.predict(...)`. It runs the model in a fresh environment and catches missing libraries early.

Serve by alias, so redeploying picks up the new champion; put the version number in the image tag so you can tell what's running.
takeaways: `mlflow models serve` answers on `/invocations` for any pyfunc model
`build-docker` packages the model and its server into a container image
Test with `mlflow models predict` in a fresh environment before deploying
pitfalls: Sending a bare list of rows to /invocations; the JSON must use a key such as dataframe_split, dataframe_records or inputs.

quiz.q: What shape of request does the /invocations endpoint accept for table data?
options: Values in the URL after a ?
JSON with a key like dataframe_split or dataframe_records
quiz.explain: The scoring server expects JSON wrapped in one of its documented keys (dataframe_split, dataframe_records, instances, inputs).

concepts.name: Evaluating classic ML models
concepts.summary: Run mlflow.models.evaluate to compute standard metrics, charts and your own metrics, and log them to a run.
concepts.why: Evaluating every model the same way makes runs comparable and catches a worse model before it is promoted.
concepts.body:
`mlflow.models.evaluate` scores a model on a **dataset** (here, a table of examples with the right answers) and logs the results to the open run:

```python
result = mlflow.models.evaluate(model_uri, eval_df, targets="label",
                                model_type="classifier")
```

- `model_type="classifier"`, for **classification** models (which pick a category), computes the standard scores: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, log loss, ROC AUC. It also logs a **confusion matrix** and ROC and precision-recall curves. `"regressor"`, for models that predict a number, computes error sizes such as MAE and RMSE, plus R2.
- `result.metrics` is a dict of values; `result.artifacts` holds the charts and tables.
- Pass `predictions="pred_col"` with `model=None` to evaluate predictions you already have, for models MLflow cannot load.
- `extra_metrics=[make_metric(eval_fn=..., greater_is_better=...)]` adds business metrics such as expected profit.

**Validation thresholds** turn evaluation into a gate: `mlflow.validate_evaluation_results(candidate_result=..., baseline_result=..., validation_thresholds={"accuracy": MetricThreshold(threshold=0.8, greater_is_better=True)})` raises an error if the new model misses a fixed bar or does worse than the current one. Run it in **CI** (the system that automatically tests every code change) before moving the `champion` alias.

For LLM and agent apps, use `mlflow.genai.evaluate` instead, which works with traces and scorers (an Expert lesson). With the `shap` library installed, `evaluator_config={"log_explainer": True}` adds charts of how much each input column pushed the predictions.

Evaluate on a fixed, versioned dataset so metrics across runs are comparable.
concepts.code:
import mlflow
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

data = load_breast_cancer(as_frame=True)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(data.data, data.target, random_state=0)
model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=5000).fit(X_tr, y_tr)

eval_df = X_te.assign(label=y_te)
with mlflow.start_run():
    info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(model, name="lr", input_example=X_te.head(2))
    result = mlflow.models.evaluate(
        info.model_uri, eval_df, targets="label", model_type="classifier")

print(round(result.metrics["accuracy_score"], 3))   # about 0.95
print("roc_auc" in result.metrics)                 # True
takeaways: `mlflow.models.evaluate` logs standard metrics and charts for each model type
Add business metrics with `extra_metrics`
Block a promotion with validation thresholds against the current model
pitfalls: Evaluating each run on a different random split of the data, which makes metric comparisons meaningless.

quiz.q: You want your automatic tests to block a model whose accuracy is worse than the current champion's. What do you use?
options: Validation thresholds comparing the new and current models' evaluation results
quiz.explain: validate_evaluation_results checks the new model's metrics against thresholds and the current model, raising an error on failure.

concepts.name: Tracing LLM and agent apps
concepts.summary: Record every LLM call, tool call and step of an AI app as a trace made of spans, automatically or with decorators.
concepts.why: LLM apps fail in non-obvious ways; traces show exactly which prompt, document search or tool call went wrong.
concepts.body:
An app built on an LLM rarely makes a single call. It may search documents, build a **prompt** (the text sent to the model), call the model, and let the model ask the app to run functions for it (**tool calling**).

A **trace** records one **request** through such an app (one question in, one answer out) as a tree of **spans**. Each span is one step: it has a name, a type (LLM, RETRIEVER for document search, TOOL, CHAIN...), inputs, outputs, timing, attributes and status. It's the same idea as **distributed tracing** in web services, and MLflow uses that field's standard format.

Three ways to create traces:

- **Autologging**: `mlflow.openai.autolog()`, `mlflow.langchain.autolog()`, `mlflow.anthropic.autolog()` and many more record LLM calls, **token** usage (LLMs read and charge for text in small chunks called tokens) and tool calls with no code changes.
- **Decorator**: `@mlflow.trace` on your own functions records their arguments and return values; decorated functions called from inside another become child spans.
- **Context manager**: `with mlflow.start_span("rerank") as span:` with `span.set_inputs(...)`, `span.set_outputs(...)`, `span.set_attribute(...)` for individual blocks of code.

Traces appear in the experiment's **Traces** tab, where you can open the span tree, see the **latency** (time taken) of each step and read the prompts. From code, `mlflow.search_traces()` returns a DataFrame for analysis, and `mlflow.get_last_active_trace_id()` gives the most recent one.

You can attach tags (user, conversation ID, app version) with `mlflow.update_current_trace(tags=...)`, and **feedback** with `mlflow.log_feedback(...)`, which later feeds evaluation.

In the live app, use the lightweight `mlflow-tracing` package and turn on **asynchronous** logging (saving traces in the background), so tracing barely slows the answers down.
takeaways: A trace is a tree of typed spans with inputs, outputs and timing
Use autologging for supported libraries and `@mlflow.trace`/`start_span` for your own code
Search, tag and add feedback to traces to find problems and evaluate the app
pitfalls: Tracing only the final LLM call, which hides retrieval or tool failures that cause most bad answers.

quiz.q: You decorate answer() and retrieve() with @mlflow.trace, and answer() calls retrieve(). How do they appear?
options: As one trace where retrieve is a child span of answer
As two runs in the experiment
quiz.explain: Nested traced calls become child spans within the same trace.

concepts.name: LoggedModels and model-centric tracking
concepts.summary: Use MLflow 3's LoggedModel to tie metrics, traces and evaluations to model versions across runs.
concepts.why: In MLflow 3 the model, not the run, is the central object, which matters for LLM apps and for choosing checkpoints.
concepts.body:
Before MLflow 3, a model was just an artifact inside a run. MLflow 3 makes the LoggedModel a first-class object with its own ID (`m-...`), parameters, metrics, tags and status, and it can be linked to several runs.

What this enables:

- **Checkpoints as models**: when training a **neural network** (a model made of many layers of learned numbers, trained epoch by epoch), you can save a **checkpoint** after each epoch with `log_model(..., step=epoch)` and log metrics with `model_id=...`. Then `mlflow.search_logged_models(filter_string="metrics.val_acc > 0.9", order_by=[...])` picks the best checkpoint directly.
- **Evaluation across runs**: evaluating an existing model in a new run links the resulting metrics back to that model's ID, so each model's page shows all its evaluations.
- **LLM app versions without learned numbers**: `mlflow.set_active_model(name="support-agent-v3")` creates or selects a LoggedModel that stands for a version of an app (its code, prompts and settings). Traces produced while it is active are linked to it, so you can compare quality and latency between app versions.

`mlflow.last_logged_model()` returns the most recent one, and `mlflow.get_logged_model(model_id)` loads its details. Model Registry versions point at LoggedModels, so you can follow the chain from the alias in use, to the model, to the training run and its dataset.

Code written for MLflow 2 (`artifact_path=`, `runs:/` addresses) mostly still works, but `artifact_path` is deprecated in favour of `name`, and new features assume model IDs.
concepts.code:
import mlflow
from sklearn.datasets import load_iris
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = load_iris(return_X_y=True, as_frame=True)
mlflow.set_experiment("checkpoints")

with mlflow.start_run():
    for i, C in enumerate([0.01, 0.1, 1.0]):
        m = LogisticRegression(C=C, max_iter=1000).fit(X, y)
        info = mlflow.sklearn.log_model(m, name=f"lr-{i}", params={"C": C},
                                        input_example=X.head(2))
        mlflow.log_metric("train_acc", m.score(X, y), model_id=info.model_id)

best = mlflow.search_logged_models(
    order_by=[{"field_name": "metrics.train_acc", "ascending": False}],
    output_format="list", max_results=1)[0]
print(best.name, best.params)   # lr-2 {'C': '1.0'}

mlflow.set_active_model(name="support-agent-v3")   # GenAI app version; traces link to it
takeaways: LoggedModel is a first-class entity with an ID, metrics and params
Log metrics with `model_id` and pick checkpoints with `search_logged_models`
`set_active_model` versions GenAI apps and links their traces
pitfalls: Sticking with artifact_path= and building paths into run artifacts by hand, instead of using the model IDs that MLflow 3 features rely on.

quiz.q: What is the main change in how MLflow 3 models relate to runs?
options: Models can no longer be linked to runs
A LoggedModel is its own entity with an ID and metrics, linkable to multiple runs
Models must be registered before they can be logged
quiz.explain: MLflow 3 makes models first-class so metrics and evaluations from many runs attach to the same model.

concepts.name: Evaluating GenAI apps with scorers
concepts.summary: Use mlflow.genai.evaluate with built-in LLM judges and your own scorers to measure and compare app versions.
concepts.why: Without systematic evaluation, prompt and model changes to LLM apps are guesswork and can quietly make things worse.
concepts.body:
`mlflow.genai.evaluate` runs your app over a set of test questions, traces each call, and applies **scorers** (functions that grade an answer) to the traces:

```python
mlflow.genai.evaluate(data=eval_data, predict_fn=my_app, scorers=[...])
```

- **data**: a list of dicts or a DataFrame with `inputs` (keyword arguments for `predict_fn`) and optional `expectations`, the known right answers, such as `expected_response` or `expected_facts`. It can also be a saved MLflow evaluation dataset or existing traces, so real traffic from the live app can be scored after the fact.
- **predict_fn**: your app; every call is traced.
- **scorers**: built-in **LLM judges** (an LLM given instructions to grade answers) such as `Correctness`, `RelevanceToQuery`, `RetrievalGroundedness`, `Safety` and `Guidelines(name=..., guidelines="...")`, or your own.

Your own scorers are functions decorated with `@scorer` that receive `inputs`, `outputs`, `expectations` and/or `trace`, and return a bool, number, string, or `Feedback` with a reason. Code-based scorers are cheap and **deterministic** (the same answer always gets the same grade), good for formats, lengths and exact checks; judges handle whether the meaning is right. `make_judge` creates your own LLM judge from plain-language instructions.

Results are logged to a run, with each row's grades attached to its trace, and the UI compares runs side by side. Judges themselves need checking: compare their verdicts with human grades on a sample before trusting them to block a release.

Registered prompts (`mlflow.genai.register_prompt`) and `set_active_model` complete the loop: change a prompt, evaluate, compare versions.
takeaways: `mlflow.genai.evaluate` = dataset + traced predict_fn + scorers
Combine cheap code scorers with LLM judges that grade whether the meaning is right
Check judges against human labels before using them as gates
pitfalls: Trusting an LLM judge's scores without checking agreement with human reviewers on a sample.

quiz.q: What does a custom @scorer function typically receive?
options: Fields such as inputs, outputs, expectations and the trace
quiz.explain: Scorers declare which of inputs, outputs, expectations and trace they need, and MLflow passes them in.

concepts.name: Operating MLflow at scale
concepts.summary: Run MLflow reliably for many teams: storage layout, access control, upgrades, cleanup and performance.
concepts.why: A shared MLflow becomes critical infrastructure; outages or lost metadata block every ML team.
concepts.body:
Running MLflow for a whole organization raises questions beyond `mlflow server`.

**Architecture.** Run several identical copies (**replicas**) of the server behind a **load balancer**, which spreads incoming requests among them. That works because the servers are **stateless**: all data lives in the database and object storage, so any copy can answer any request.

Use a managed PostgreSQL or MySQL database for the backend store. Consider separate artifact-only servers (`--artifacts-only`) when big model uploads would slow everything else down. On Kubernetes, the community Helm charts are the usual starting point.

**Access control.** The built-in username-and-password mode (`--app-name basic-auth`) supports users and per-experiment and per-model permissions (READ, EDIT, MANAGE). Larger setups put a **single sign-on** gateway (one company login for every tool) in front, or use workspaces to keep teams apart on one server. Managed platforms (Databricks, SageMaker, Azure ML, Nebius) offer hosted MLflow with sign-in built in.

**Upgrades.** New versions may change the database schema. Back up the database, then run `mlflow db upgrade <backend-uri>` before starting new servers. Old clients usually keep working against newer servers, but test before rolling out.

**Cleanup.** Deleting runs or experiments only marks them deleted. `mlflow gc --backend-store-uri ... --older-than 30d` removes them and their artifacts for good. Set rules for how long checkpoints and large artifacts are kept.

**Performance.** The metrics table grows fastest. Log per-step metrics at sensible intervals, send several at once with `log_metrics` (a **batch**), and turn on asynchronous logging (`MLFLOW_ENABLE_ASYNC_LOGGING=true`) so training doesn't wait on the network. Broad `search_runs` calls over huge experiments should fetch results page by page.
concepts.code:
# Shell (operations):
#   mlflow db upgrade postgresql://mlflow:pw@db:5432/mlflow      # after backup
#   mlflow gc --backend-store-uri postgresql://mlflow:pw@db:5432/mlflow --older-than 30d
#   mlflow server --app-name basic-auth --workers 4 \
#       --backend-store-uri postgresql://mlflow:pw@db:5432/mlflow \
#       --artifacts-destination s3://acme-ml-artifacts
import mlflow

mlflow.config.enable_async_logging(True)       # don't block training on logging I/O
with mlflow.start_run():
    for step in range(0, 1000, 100):            # log at intervals, not every step
        mlflow.log_metrics({"loss": 1 / (step + 1), "lr": 1e-3}, step=step)
mlflow.flush_async_logging()
print("logged 10 batched points per metric")
takeaways: Stateless servers + a managed PostgreSQL/MySQL database + object storage is the standard layout
Back up, then `mlflow db upgrade`, before running a new server version
Deleted runs need `mlflow gc` to be removed; log metrics in batches and asynchronously
pitfalls: Upgrading the MLflow server package without running the database migration, which makes the server fail to start or behave inconsistently.

quiz.q: Users deleted thousands of old runs but storage did not shrink. Why?
options: Artifacts are stored in the database
Deletion is soft; mlflow gc must be run to purge runs and artifacts
quiz.explain: Deleted runs are only marked deleted until garbage collection permanently removes them.
